keywords: how do i target an element
entries.response: .account-card { property: value; } — the dot before a name matches an HTML class attribute. Without the dot, it tries to match a tag name that doesn't exist, and silently does nothing.

Check the selector spelling matches the class name exactly, including the leading dot. Also check for a missing semicolon on an earlier line — one missing semicolon can silently break every property after it in that block.
background: #1a1f29; (or any colour you like — named colours like 'navy' work too) sets the fill behind the element's content.
border-radius: 12px; rounds all four corners by that amount — bigger number, more rounded.
padding: 24px; adds space between the content and the edge of its own box. margin does the same thing but on the outside, between this box and others nearby.
font-weight: 700; (or font-weight: bold;) makes text bold. 400 is normal weight, 700 and above reads as bold.
display: flex; on a container arranges its direct children in a row instead of stacked on top of each other. It has to go on the parent, not the items inside it.
The single most common flexbox mistake: display: flex needs to be on the container (the parent), not on the items you're trying to lay out. Check which selector it's attached to.
justify-content: space-between; pushes the first item to the left edge and the last to the right edge, spreading anything in between evenly.
align-items: center; centres items vertically within a flex row — useful when items are different heights and you want them lined up in the middle.

Scroll the CSS editor — all four sections (Header, Nav, Card, Transaction List) are listed as comments in one file. Work through them in any order; nothing you write gets erased when you move to the next one.
gap: 16px; adds space between flex items without needing margin on each individual one — much simpler when you've got several items in a row.
